strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: reducing dependence on scarce, privacy-sensitive indoor 3D annotations by learning from readily available house-tour videos.
The proposed pipeline combines video curation, Dust3R-based reconstruction, semantic labeling, voxelization, and region-level 2D-to-3D distillation into a conceptually coherent workflow.
Region-level alignment using matched superpixels and supervoxels is intuitive for cluttered indoor scenes and requires little modification to the downstream occupancy architecture.

The experiments cover NYUv2 and OccScanNet, including full-data, label-efficient, cross-dataset, and zero-shot settings. The largest result—+5.25 mIoU on NYUv2 with 10% labels—suggests that the pretraining can be useful when annotations are scarce.
The manuscript is generally easy to follow, and the qualitative results provide some visual evidence of improved object completion.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the scientific evidence is insufficient to establish the proposed method's effectiveness. There are no component ablations comparing region-level distillation against pixel-level or global distillation, removing SAN masks, alternative 2D teachers, or pretraining without YouTube-Occ. Only one occupancy backbone is tested despite the claim that the method is model-agnostic.

The abstract claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on both benchmarks, but Table 5 reports only the proposed model, with low scores of 9.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and 4.61 mIoU on OccScanNet. Without any zero-shot baselines, the state-of-the-art claim is unsupported.

Several quantitative statements are incorrect or contradictory. For OccScanNet, the manuscript claims gains of +15.75, +12.04, and +9.95 for television, object, and furniture, whereas Table 2 shows gains over Symphonies of only +0.35, +0.35, and +0.08. Figure 5 reports a +0.45 mIoU full-data gain although Table 2 and the accompanying text give 58.15−57.85=+0.30. In Table 4, 50%-label IoU decreases from 55.90 to 55.77, contradicting the claim of consistent improvement.

The strongest OccScanNet gains are only about 0.25–0.30 points, yet results are reported from single runs without error bars or significance analysis. It is therefore unclear whether these improvements exceed normal training variability. Even several cross-dataset gains are extremely small.

The central YouTube-Occ resource is not adequately validated or reproducible. The paper provides no quantitative reconstruction, camera-pose, depth, scale, or semantic-label accuracy evaluation; no class, geographic, scene-diversity, or failure statistics; and no analysis of the heuristic assumption that walls are 2.8 meters high. The dataset will explicitly not be released, while collection queries, channel lists, clip splitting rules, filtering thresholds, and sufficient reconstruction parameters are also omitted.

Dataset protocols are unclear. Frame-level YouTube-Occ train/validation splitting may place frames from the same video or physical property in both splits. The paper mentions a scene-disjoint resplit of OccScanNet but does not clearly identify which tables use it; the markedly different score ranges across Tables 2 and 4 make comparisons difficult to interpret.

The data-usage discussion is inadequate for scraped house-tour footage. The manuscript does not document YouTube terms, video licenses, uploader consent, privacy filtering, or safeguards beyond withholding the derived dataset. The checklist even labels the work as introducing no new asset despite presenting YouTube-Occ as a principal contribution.

Important implementation details are missing, including exact clip construction, frame sampling, point-cloud filters and thresholds, axis/floor estimation, metric scaling, cropping into the fixed 60×60×36 grid, handling of missing or conflicting regions, temperature and projection-head settings, and preprocessing cost. The stated compute information gives GPU count but not runtime, memory, or dataset-generation cost.

The paper overstates conclusions from modest evidence: full-data gains are small, zero-shot transfer is weak, and no comparison isolates whether benefits arise from the proposed loss, generic DINOv2 initialization, reconstructed web geometry, or simply additional frames. These issues collectively prevent a convincing case for acceptance despite the promising direction.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: obtaining scalable pretraining data for monocular indoor 3D semantic occupancy without calibrated capture hardware.
The proposed pipeline—house-tour video curation, DUSt3R reconstruction, foundation-model masks/features, and superpixel–supervoxel contrastive alignment—is intuitive and potentially useful.
Experiments cover NYUv2 and OccScanNet, including low-label transfer. The strongest results are the NYUv2 low-label gains and the +2.47 mIoU improvement on OccScanNet with 1% labels.
The approach requires little modification to the Symphonies backbone, and the paper reports basic optimization settings, hardware, and qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The submission also makes a substantial dataset contribution; under a Datasets/Benchmarks assessment it would fare worse because YouTube-Occ will not be released and is documented too sparsely for independent use or verification.

The abstract's claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance is unsupported. The zero-shot results are only 9.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and 4.61 on OccScanNet, are presented without any zero-shot baselines, and are explicitly described later as limited. The reported state-of-the-art numbers instead require supervised fine-tuning on the target datasets.

The experimental evidence does not isolate the contributions. There are no ablations for superpixel-level versus pixel-level alignment, the contrastive objective, SAN masks, DINOv2 features, YouTube-Occ versus ordinary in-domain pretraining, dataset size, or reconstruction/filtering choices. Consequently, it is unclear which component produces the gains.

Most full-data gains are small: +1.04 mIoU on NYUv2 and +0.30 on OccScanNet. There are no repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests, so these improvements may fall within training variance. Table 4 even shows lower IoU at 50% labels (55.77 versus 55.90), contradicting the claim of a consistent advantage across all settings.

The reliability of the automatically generated 3D supervision is not evaluated. Camera poses, depth, alignment, and scale all inherit DUSt3R errors, while metric scale is imposed through the crude assumption that walls are 2.8 m high. The paper provides no reconstruction accuracy study, manual audit, failure rate, retained-data statistics, or analysis connecting pseudo-label quality to downstream performance.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a central web-data contribution. The 651 clips and 14,592 frames will not be released; video IDs and precise collection criteria are absent; several heuristic filters and preprocessing operations lack parameters; and the paper does not specify enough implementation detail for the feature projections, normalization, sampling, or contrastive negatives.

The method is technically plausible but fairly incremental, combining existing reconstruction, segmentation, feature extraction, and contrastive distillation components. Without ablations or stronger comparisons, the paper does not establish that the proposed region-level formulation is original or superior to simpler alternatives.

Dataset governance is insufficiently addressed. The manuscript does not discuss YouTube terms, copyright, uploader consent, licenses, geographic or socioeconomic biases, or privacy risks from reconstructing interiors of real homes. The checklist incorrectly states that no new asset is introduced and claims broader impacts are discussed when the provided text does not meaningfully analyze them.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies and overstatements, alongside unclear notation and section cross-references. The limitation discussion mentions only dynamic objects and omits the much more important issues of noisy geometry, heuristic scaling, domain bias, non-release, and privacy.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in indoor semantic occupancy prediction: obtaining diverse 3D training data without calibrated capture hardware or manual voxel annotation. Using house-tour videos is practical and potentially impactful.

The automated pipeline combining clip curation, Dust3R reconstruction, semantic labeling, filtering, alignment, and voxelization is coherent. Region-level superpixel–supervoxel distillation is also intuitively better suited to cluttered indoor scenes than unconstrained pixel-level matching.

The evaluation covers NYUv2 and OccScanNet, full-data and label-efficient fine-tuning, cross-dataset transfer from YouTube-Occ, and zero-shot transfer. The low-label improvements are promising: gains reach 5.25 mIoU on NYUv2 with 10% labels, 4.21 mIoU when pretraining on YouTube-Occ, and 2.47 mIoU on OccScanNet with 1% labels.
Using the same Symphonies backbone for the main controlled comparisons helps isolate the benefit of pretraining. The method improves the baseline consistently across most reported settings.

The paper is generally easy to follow, and the pipeline and qualitative figures communicate the motivation and approach effectively. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the work also has a substantial Applied/Systems and dataset component.
weaknesses: The central experimental evidence lacks essential ablations. There is no comparison against pixel-level or global distillation, pretraining without SAN masks, alternative reconstruction or masking models, different amounts of YouTube data, or supervised pseudo-label pretraining. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that the proposed region-level formulation is responsible for the gains.

The headline claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance is unsupported. Table 5 reports only the proposed model, with no zero-shot baselines, and the paper itself characterizes the resulting 9.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and 4.61 mIoU on OccScanNet as limited. This claim should be removed or substantiated with comparable methods and identical evaluation protocols.

Many full-data improvements are small—0.30 mIoU and 0.25 IoU over Symphonies on OccScanNet—and no repeated runs, error bars, or significance analysis are provided. The manuscript also contains numerical errors: it claims OccScanNet improvements of 15.75, 12.04, and 9.95 points for television, object, and furniture, whereas Table 2 shows gains of only 0.35, 0.35, and 0.08 points. Figure 5 likewise labels the 57.85-to-58.15 gain as 0.45 rather than 0.30 mIoU.

The quality of YouTube-Occ's automatically generated geometry and semantics is not evaluated. There are no reconstruction-error measurements, pseudo-label accuracy estimates, manual audits, failure rates, dataset diversity statistics, or comparisons before and after filtering. This is particularly important given the heuristic 2.8-meter wall-height scaling and the accumulation of Dust3R, alignment, filtering, and SAN errors.

YouTube-Occ is central to the claimed contribution but will explicitly not be released. The paper also omits video identifiers, detailed collection criteria, licenses, YouTube terms-of-service considerations, and meaningful privacy analysis. Thus, neither the dataset nor the main cross-dataset results are independently reproducible, despite the checklist's reproducibility and licensing claims.

Important implementation details are missing, including filter thresholds, clip construction parameters, coordinate alignment procedure, crop/origin conventions, feature normalization and projection, temperature, negative sampling scope, handling of empty or invalid regions, and total preprocessing/training time. The claim that the method is model-agnostic is tested only with Symphonies.

The limitations and broader-impact discussion is inadequate. It mentions only dynamic objects and non-release, while overlooking reconstruction failures, domain bias toward real-estate footage, privacy and copyright risks in scraped home videos, dependence on proprietary or pretrained components, and sensitivity to scale estimation. Overall, the idea and preliminary transfer results are encouraging, but the missing controls, unsupported claims, numerical inconsistencies, and inability to verify the main data contribution slightly outweigh the merits.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in indoor 3D semantic occupancy: scarce, costly, and privacy-sensitive annotated 3D data. Using uncalibrated web videos is a practically meaningful direction with potential impact beyond this task.

YouTube-Occ is substantial in scale, comprising 100,372 frames from 5,241 scenes. The pipeline combines video filtering, DUSt3R reconstruction, SAN semantic labeling, metric-scale normalization, and occupancy voxelization into a coherent data-generation workflow.

The proposed distillation framework is compatible with multiple occupancy architectures. Improvements are demonstrated for MonoScene, Symphonies, and EmbodiedOcc, spanning CNN-, voxel-transformer-, and Gaussian-transformer-based models.

Results are consistent across NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet. For example, Symphonies improves from 29.70 to 31.65 mIoU on NYUv2 and from 47.71 to 49.38 on Occ-ScanNet. The few-shot experiments are particularly compelling, with YouTube-Occ pre-training providing gains of 3.29 and 5.09 mIoU using 5% and 10% of NYUv2 labels.

The authors appropriately show that naive pseudo-label supervision performs poorly, motivating the feature-level approach rather than hiding the low quality of the generated occupancy labels. Component and design ablations support the region loss, prototype loss, Gaussianization, and prototype momentum choices.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and its qualitative results illustrate more coherent scene completion after pre-training.
weaknesses: The main evidence does not cleanly disentangle the value of web data from the value of the proposed distillation objective and foundation-model teachers. In-domain pre-training is consistently stronger than YouTube-Occ pre-training, while comparisons against alternative pre-training strategies are reported only on NYUv2. Controls using matched quantities of target-domain videos, generic non-curated videos, or the same data with alternative distillation objectives would sharpen the central claim.

Method and dataset construction details are insufficient for strong reproducibility. The manuscript omits the precise video/channel selection procedure, clip and frame sampling rules, filtering heuristics, DUSt3R cleanup and orientation algorithms, handling of failed reconstructions and overlapping or absent semantic masks, Gaussian rasterization/compositing details, loss temperatures, and several training schedules.

There is limited analysis of the generated dataset itself. Beyond aggregate size and an Occ-ScanNet pseudo-label score of only 10.06 mIoU, the paper provides no category distribution, geographic or visual diversity statistics, reconstruction success rate, per-class pseudo-label quality, failure analysis, deduplication or benchmark-contamination check, or sensitivity to the assumed 2.8 m wall height.

The algorithmic ingredients—2D feature distillation, Gaussian rendering, contrastive region alignment, and EMA class prototypes—are individually established. Their integration is useful, but the technical originality is moderate, and comparisons to the most closely related self-supervised occupancy approaches discussed in Section 4.3 are largely qualitative rather than experimental.

Reported improvements are based on single numbers without repeated runs, error bars, or significance analysis. Some full-data gains are modest, such as 0.76 mIoU from web pre-training on Occ-ScanNet, making variance information important.

The SOTA framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence warrants: comparisons mix different architectures, and the paper does not report standardized compute, backbone, pre-training budget, or all architecture-dataset combinations. Pre-training cost and inference/training overhead are also absent.

Because the dataset derives from YouTube real-estate videos, a release requires careful treatment of copyright, platform terms, privacy, consent, faces or personal information, and takedown procedures. The manuscript promises public data release but does not describe licensing, redistribution policy, anonymization, or broader ethical safeguards.

strengths: The central direction is relevant and potentially impactful: using abundant, uncalibrated web videos to reduce dependence on costly indoor 3D annotations addresses a genuine bottleneck in semantic occupancy prediction.
The paper assembles a complete pipeline—video filtering, Dust3R-based reconstruction, SAN-derived semantics, voxelization, and representation pre-training—and evaluates it on NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet.

The reported improvements are reasonably consistent across three substantially different architectures. For example, pre-training improves Symphonies from 29.70 to 31.65 mIoU on NYUv2 and from 47.71 to 49.38 on Occ-ScanNet. The few-label results also suggest that pre-training is most useful when annotations are scarce.
The component ablations support both region and prototype alignment, and the 50K-versus-100K comparison provides limited evidence of a beneficial data-scaling trend.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared. I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution with a supporting pre-training method, because the most distinctive claim is the 100,372-frame YouTube-Occ resource. Under that framing, the dataset evidence and documentation are inadequate: there is no detailed source/channel inventory, license or redistribution plan, train/validation partition, duplicate analysis, scene-definition procedure, geographic or visual-diversity characterization, failure-rate accounting, or systematic quality audit.

The paper does not convincingly isolate the value of the proposed web-data pipeline. The losses primarily distill DINOv2 features within SAN-generated semantic regions, and it is unclear how much the reconstructed occupancy pseudo-labels themselves contribute. There is no comparison using the same distillation method on generic indoor images, randomly selected web videos, or data processed without the full reconstruction and pseudo-label pipeline.

The pseudo-label quality is very low—10.06 mIoU and 27.00 IoU on Occ-ScanNet—and direct or joint supervised use can hurt performance. This is an important finding, but the paper supplies only three qualitative examples and no classwise quality, reconstruction accuracy, camera-pose error, scale-error distribution, filtering precision, or retained-video statistics. Consequently, the claimed reliability and scalability of the automated pipeline are not established.

Several technical details needed to understand or reproduce the method are missing. The manuscript does not specify how absent or empty semantic masks enter Eqs. 2–3, how prototypes are initialized and synchronized, how free and unknown voxels are treated, the rendering and visibility settings, filtering heuristics, floor/wall detection and scale normalization procedure, video sampling policy, or the exact adaptation of competing training strategies.

Experimental controls are insufficient for the modest gains. Results are reported from apparently single runs, including highly variable 5% and 10% label regimes, without standard deviations or fixed split details. There is no compute-matched control for extra pre-training, no ablation of DINOv2 versus SAN versus reconstructed geometry, and no equal-size comparison between web and in-domain pre-training data. MonoScene is evaluated on only one of the two benchmarks.

The comparison set does not adequately substantiate broad superiority. Despite discussing recent self-supervised occupancy methods such as GaussTR, AutoOcc, SelfOcc, and S4C, the experiments compare mainly against auxiliary losses and Pri3D, with little explanation of adaptation or fairness. The claim of learning robust, generalizable 3D priors is therefore stronger than the evidence, which covers only two closely related indoor benchmarks with the same class taxonomy and voxel specification.

The data collection raises unresolved reproducibility and societal concerns. Real-estate videos can reveal private home interiors, and the paper offers no discussion of consent, copyright, YouTube terms, personally identifying content, removal requests, or bias in the available housing footage. This omission is especially notable because privacy is used as a motivation for the work.

Overall, the idea and initial results have merit, but the central causal claim—that the curated uncalibrated web-video resource and its reconstructed 3D information drive the improvements—is not demonstrated. The missing dataset audit, method details, controlled baselines, and uncertainty analysis are consequential rather than minor presentation issues.

strengths: This is a timely, practically relevant data-centric contribution: YouTube-Occ turns uncalibrated web videos into pretraining data for indoor semantic occupancy, addressing a genuine scarcity and privacy bottleneck. Because no contribution type is explicitly declared, I assess it as Algorithms/General, while recognizing that much of its value is an Applied/Systems-style combination of automated data curation and representation learning. The integrated pipeline using Dust3R, SAN, voxelization, and web-video filtering is novel and potentially impactful even though its individual ingredients are established.

The proposed dual-alignment framework is technically sensible: voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering enables local 3D-to-2D feature alignment, while momentum class prototypes encourage cross-scene semantic consistency. Component ablations show that both losses contribute and that their combination performs best.

The empirical evidence is broad in important dimensions. Improvements are demonstrated on NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet and across three materially different architectures—MonoScene, Symphonies, and EmbodiedOcc—supporting the model-agnostic claim.

The limited-label results are particularly compelling: YouTube-Occ pretraining improves NYUv2 mIoU by 3.29 and 5.09 points at the 5% and 10% splits, respectively, and the full 100K-frame corpus consistently exceeds its 50K subset. Full-data improvements are smaller but consistent, with Symphonies gaining 1.95 mIoU on NYUv2 and 1.67 on Occ-ScanNet under in-domain pretraining, and web-data pretraining also improving both benchmarks.

The paper is generally clear, motivates why naive pseudo-label supervision fails, includes comparisons with alternative training strategies, and openly acknowledges limitations involving occluded voxels, temporal modeling, and the fixed wall-height assumption.
weaknesses: The web-data construction is not documented adequately for reproducibility or auditing. Important missing details include the number and selection of source videos/channels, clip length and frame sampling, exact filtering and reconstruction heuristics, failure/rejection rates, scene deduplication, and checks for overlap with downstream benchmarks.

The dataset discussion omits licensing, redistribution, creator consent, privacy screening, and demographic/geographic bias. These issues are especially relevant because the paper motivates web video as a scalable solution to privacy-sensitive indoor data and promises to release the resulting data.

The evaluation does not fully isolate what makes the proposed web corpus effective. A controlled baseline that applies the same distillation objective to ordinary unlabeled target-domain images, web images without reconstructed pseudo-geometry, or a size-matched alternative indoor corpus would better separate benefits from web-video scale, temporal reconstruction, and the proposed losses.

The strongest in-domain pretraining remains better than YouTube-Occ across all entries in Table 3. This does not negate the contribution, but it tempers claims of broad generalization and indicates a remaining domain gap. Evaluation on an additional out-of-domain dataset or different geographic/interior style would strengthen the central scalability claim.

Full-data gains are modest, and the manuscript reports neither repeated runs nor uncertainty estimates. This matters for improvements such as 0.76 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet with YouTube-Occ pretraining and for comparisons among closely spaced methods.

Several implementation details needed to reproduce the method are absent or underspecified, including prototype initialization and the precise update rule, feature normalization, temperatures, loss weighting, treatment of absent or overlapping semantic masks, rasterization settings, opacity-network design, and the pretraining schedule. The promised code and data release helps prospectively but does not replace these details in the manuscript.

The novelty lies primarily in the integration and adaptation of existing reconstruction, segmentation, Gaussian rendering, and prototype-contrastive ideas. The comparison with prior pretraining is limited mainly to Pri3D on NYUv2; broader and compute-matched comparisons to recent foundation-model-aligned occupancy methods would make the originality and efficiency case more convincing.
